reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: A congenital variant in which a segment of coronary artery, most often the left anterior descending, tunnels through myocardium instead of lying on the epicardial surface
During systole the overlying muscle compresses the bridged segment, producing the classic angiographic milking effect
It is common and usually benign, discovered incidentally, but in some patients it causes angina, ischaemia, or arrhythmia
Because coronary filling is mainly diastolic, symptoms tend to relate to tachycardia and shortened diastole rather than the systolic compression alone
Symptoms may be provoked by exertion, and there are reported associations with arrhythmia and, rarely, with acute coronary events
Coronary angiography, CT coronary angiography, and intracoronary imaging or physiological assessment can characterise the bridge and its functional significance
Treatment usually begins with agents that reduce heart rate and contractility to prolong diastolic filling, reserving invasive options for refractory cases
Nitrates may worsen symptoms by accentuating the appearance and effect of the bridge, an important prescribing consideration
reference.pathophysiology: Myocardial bridging occurs when a coronary artery, rather than running entirely over the epicardium, dips into and is covered by a band of myocardium along part of its course. Contraction of this overlying muscle compresses the tunnelled segment during systole and, in significant cases, delayed relaxation prolongs compression into early diastole when most coronary perfusion occurs. This dynamic narrowing can reduce flow and, together with endothelial dysfunction and increased susceptibility to spasm at the bridge, contribute to myocardial ischaemia, particularly when heart rate rises and diastole shortens.
additionalDifferentials: Anomalous coronary artery origin or course
additionalInvestigations: Coronary angiography demonstrating systolic compression of the tunnelled segment
CT coronary angiography to define the bridge depth and length
Intravascular imaging and intracoronary physiological assessment for functional significance
Stress testing to detect inducible ischaemia
Echocardiography to exclude associated structural disease
Ambulatory monitoring when arrhythmia is suspected
redFlags: Angina at rest or crescendo symptoms suggesting an acute coronary syndrome
Documented myocardial ischaemia or infarction attributable to the bridge
Exertional syncope or serious ventricular arrhythmia
Symptoms refractory to appropriate medical therapy
reference.prognosis: The overall prognosis is generally good, as most bridges are asymptomatic and benign. When symptomatic, many patients respond well to medical therapy that lengthens diastolic perfusion time; a minority with deep or long bridges and refractory ischaemia may require invasive intervention, and outcomes are then influenced by the anatomy and any coexisting coronary disease.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to a bridge without confirming ischaemia or excluding other causes
Prescribing nitrates, which can aggravate rather than relieve bridge-related symptoms
Overlooking associated fixed atherosclerotic disease proximal to the bridge
Assuming an incidental bridge fully explains atypical chest pain
Proceeding to invasive treatment before optimising medical therapy
